extracted.intended_audience: biomedical researchers, NIH-funded investigators, policy analysts, and others interested in NIH funding equity
extracted.subtask_short: blog commentary on NIH funding disparity
extracted.subtask_description: A short blog post commenting on a GAO report about racial and ethnic disparities in NIH grant funding, contrasting metrics used (applicant-level vs application-level) and noting that disparities persist despite NIH actions post-Ginther. Intended as commentary for researchers and policy watchers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choice of metric for measuring funding disparity
rubrics_metrics.description: Distinguish whether the reported data are by 'applicant funding rate' (applicant PI) or by 'success rate of applications' (application-level). The Ginther data focused on the success rate of applications from PIs of various groups; the GAO report data are described mostly as the applicant funding rate or similar.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be explicit which denominator is used when reporting disparities: applicant-level vs application-level. The page notes that 'if these data are by applicant PI and not by applications, there will be some small differences.' Even if differences are small, specify metric to avoid misinterpretation and to allow accurate comparison with earlier analyses (e.g., Ginther).

rubrics_metrics.name: Assessing progress on workforce diversity goals
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate whether NIH actions taken since the Ginther report have reduced funding disparities for underrepresented racial and ethnic groups. The GAO report 'recit[es] the supposed steps NIH has been taking in the wake of the Ginther report in 2011' but presents updated evidence (Figure 2) showing the disparity remains.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use updated depictions (figures, trends) to judge whether policy steps have led to measurable improvement. Do not rely solely on recitations of actions—compare them against outcome metrics (funding rates) over time to determine effectiveness.
